author: san diego city wire
title: San Diego County issues guidance after coyote attack injures two children - San Diego City Wire
text:
A recent coyote attack near the UTC mall on November 25, 2025, which resulted in injuries to two children, has led San Diego County and its partner agencies to take action to protect public safety. The County is working to educate residents about how to prevent coyotes from becoming accustomed to humans and what steps to take if they encounter one.
County Animal Services recommends a technique called “coyote hazing” for those who come across a coyote. This method aims to reinforce the animal’s natural fear of people and discourage it from returning to populated areas. Residents are advised that if a coyote approaches, they should use hazing methods until the animal leaves the area. If the coyote does not move away, taking a few steps forward and repeating the behavior is suggested.
In cases where someone is bitten by a coyote, immediate emergency medical care should be sought. Rabies post-exposure treatment is generally not available at regular medical offices.
Coyotes often enter neighborhoods due to attractants such as pet food or water left outside, unsecured trash cans, or fallen fruit from trees. Removing these items can help reduce visits from wildlife. Homeowners can also install devices like “coyote rollers” on top of fences; these tubes spin when climbed on, preventing coyotes from gaining traction and getting over the fence.
County Animal Services provides 24-hour response in unincorporated areas of San Diego County when animals pose a public safety risk. Residents living within incorporated cities are advised to contact their local animal services provider for assistance.
While rabies is rare among coyotes, it remains a serious disease spread through bites, making it important for residents to avoid contact with aggressive animals and report such incidents.
The County does not respond to reports of wildlife that are simply roaming or causing minor nuisances—such as skunks under porches or opossums accessing pet food—but will act when there is an imminent threat.
When visiting parks or preserves, dog owners are encouraged to keep pets leashed and close by. Small dogs should be picked up immediately if a coyote is seen nearby since leaving them on the ground could provoke a chase response. Cats should be kept indoors whenever possible.
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife notes that coyotes play an important role in controlling rodent populations within local ecosystems. Understanding how to safely coexist with these animals is considered essential.
More information about wildlife safety can be found at www.sddac.com or by calling (619) 767-2675.
